titlePl: Matura PR: Praca — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Work — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Praca na maturę rozszerzoną: rynek pracy, umowy, kariera i prawa pracownika. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended Matura Work: labour market, contracts, careers and workers' rights.

items.definitionEn: relating to office or professional work rather than manual labour
items.example: White-collar roles in finance still cluster in the capital.

items.definitionEn: relating to manual or industrial work, often paid by the hour
items.example: Blue-collar jobs in the shipyard vanished within a decade.

items.definitionEn: the part of the economy run by government, such as schools and hospitals
items.example: Pay in the public sector lagged behind prices for three years.

items.definitionEn: businesses owned by individuals or companies, not by the state
items.example: She left teaching for a private sector consultancy.

items.definitionEn: charities, social enterprises and other not-for-profit organisations
items.example: The third sector relies on short grants and tired volunteers.

items.definitionEn: a person employed by the state to run public administration
items.example: A government official must remain politically impartial at work.

items.definitionEn: someone whose main capital is expertise, analysis or design rather than physical labour
items.example: The knowledge worker can often work from anywhere with a laptop.

items.definitionEn: the sector that makes physical goods in factories
items.example: The manufacturing industry still employs thousands in Silesia.

items.definitionEn: the sector that provides services rather than goods, such as retail or hospitality
items.example: The service industry recovered faster than heavy industry.

items.definitionEn: work sold in short tasks via apps, with little job security
items.example: The gig economy offers flexibility and almost no sick pay.

items.definitionEn: the supply of and demand for paid work in an economy
items.example: A tight labour market pushed starting salaries up.

items.definitionEn: all the people available for or engaged in work in a place
items.example: An ageing workforce means more people will retire together.

items.definitionEn: workers trained in a trade or technical craft
items.example: Skilled labour is scarce in heating and ventilation.

items.definitionEn: jobs that need little formal training on day one
items.example: Unskilled work is often the first to be automated.

items.definitionEn: work done mainly with the hands and body
items.example: Years of manual labour left him with a damaged back.

items.definitionEn: office work such as filing, data entry and correspondence
items.example: A clerical job was the stepping stone to office management.

items.definitionEn: managers between senior leaders and front-line staff
items.example: Middle management was the first layer cut in the merger.

items.definitionEn: the group of directors and heads who set strategy
items.example: Senior management froze recruitment until spring.

items.definitionEn: the group legally responsible for governing a company
items.example: The board of directors rejected the takeover bid.

items.definitionEn: the highest-ranking manager running a company day to day
items.example: The chief executive resigned after the safety inquiry.

items.definitionEn: the person you report to in the everyday hierarchy
items.example: Raise the problem with your line manager before you escalate it.

items.definitionEn: the department that hires, pays and supports staff
items.example: Human resources sent a revised handbook in January.

items.definitionEn: an organisation that sets standards and entry rules for a profession
items.example: The professional body can strike a doctor off the register.

items.definitionEn: a practical occupation learnt through apprenticeship, such as plumbing
items.example: A skilled trade can pay more than some graduate office posts.

items.definitionEn: the small group of applicants chosen for the last stage of recruitment
items.example: Only four names made the shortlist for the editorship.

items.definitionEn: a recruiter paid to approach people already in work for a vacancy
items.example: A headhunter rang her about a role she had not seen advertised.

items.definitionEn: the first months in a job when either side may end it more easily
items.example: The probation period lasts six months in this firm.

items.definitionEn: an official outline of duties, seniority and working conditions
items.example: The job description said nothing about weekend work.

items.definitionEn: the skills, qualifications and traits an employer says it wants
items.example: Match your evidence to every point on the person specification.

items.definitionEn: a timed test of reasoning, numbers or language used in recruitment
items.example: The aptitude test eliminated half the applicants before interview.

items.definitionEn: questionnaires that claim to measure personality or ability for hiring
items.example: Psychometric testing should never be the only selection tool.

items.definitionEn: a recruitment day of tasks, tests and interviews used to compare candidates
items.example: The assessment centre included a group negotiation and a case study.

items.definitionEn: an interview conducted by several people at once
items.example: A panel interview feels formal, so prepare a concise opening.

items.definitionEn: an interview that asks for evidence of skills through past examples
items.example: In a competency-based interview, use a clear situation-action-result story.

items.definitionEn: enquiries into identity, qualifications or criminal record before hiring
items.example: The background check delayed her start date by a fortnight.

items.definitionEn: official permission for a foreign national to take a job
items.example: Without a work permit he could not take the laboratory post.

items.definitionEn: a formal proposal of employment, usually in writing
items.example: Read the job offer twice before you sign.

items.definitionEn: to refuse a job or contract that has been proposed
items.example: She had to turn down an offer that clashed with her studies.

items.definitionEn: a firm paid to find candidates for employers
items.example: The recruitment agency took a fee from the employer, not from her.

items.definitionEn: contacting an employer who has not advertised a vacancy
items.example: A speculative application led to a two-month trial.

items.definitionEn: building professional contacts who may share information or openings
items.example: Networking at the conference mattered more than the keynote.

items.definitionEn: abilities useful in more than one job or sector
items.example: Teaching gave her transferable skills in presentation and planning.

items.definitionEn: interpersonal abilities such as communication, teamwork and empathy
items.example: Soft skills decide who is trusted with clients.

items.definitionEn: teachable technical abilities such as coding, accounting or welding
items.example: Hard skills can be certified; judgement still comes with practice.

items.definitionEn: the structured process of settling a new employee into the organisation
items.example: Onboarding lasted a week and still missed the software passwords.

items.definitionEn: a planned introduction to rules, people and systems at the start of a job
items.example: The induction programme includes a fire walk and data-protection training.

items.definitionEn: following an experienced worker to learn what the role involves
items.example: A day of job shadowing put her off warehouse management.

items.definitionEn: a structured traineeship for people with degrees, rotating through departments
items.example: The graduate scheme rotates through three countries in two years.

items.definitionEn: a short period of work, paid or unpaid, to gain experience
items.example: The summer internship led to a graduate post.

items.definitionEn: a temporary move to another team or organisation while remaining employed
items.example: A six-month secondment to Brussels changed her career plans.

items.definitionEn: an employment contract with no planned end date
items.example: She waited two years for a permanent contract after a chain of temp posts.

items.definitionEn: working for several clients rather than as a single company's employee
items.example: He went freelance after the agency cut his hours.

items.definitionEn: a contract with no guaranteed hours, called in only when needed
items.example: A zero-hours contract makes rent almost impossible to plan.

items.definitionEn: a contract that ends on a stated date unless renewed
items.example: The fixed-term contract runs until the grant expires in March.

items.definitionEn: irregular paid work with no expectation of ongoing hours
items.example: Casual work in hospitality filled the summer but not the winter.

items.definitionEn: the legal agreement setting out pay, duties and conditions of a job
items.example: Do not start until the employment contract is signed.

items.definitionEn: the detailed rules of an employment contract, including pay, hours and notice
items.example: Hidden contractual terms allowed unpaid weekend duty.

items.definitionEn: the time you or the employer must give before the job ends
items.example: The notice period is three months for managers.

items.definitionEn: remaining employed and paid while being kept away from work during notice
items.example: Garden leave stopped him taking clients to a rival firm.

items.definitionEn: a contract term restricting work for rivals after you leave
items.example: The non-compete clause was too broad to enforce.

items.definitionEn: a term forbidding the sharing of the employer's private information
items.example: The confidentiality clause survives after you resign.

items.definitionEn: two people splitting the duties and hours of one full-time post
items.example: Job-sharing let both parents collect children from school.

items.definitionEn: working a full week's hours in fewer, longer days
items.example: Compressed hours give her a regular weekday off.

items.definitionEn: a contract that sets hours for the year, with busy and quiet periods
items.example: Annualised hours suit a hotel that is full only in summer.

items.definitionEn: doing your job away from the employer's premises, usually from home
items.example: Remote working saved her three hours of commuting a day.

items.definitionEn: a mix of days in the workplace and days working remotely
items.example: Hybrid working still requires two core days in the office.

items.definitionEn: sharing desks as they become free rather than having a personal one
items.example: Hot-desking made confidential calls almost impossible.

items.definitionEn: paying another firm to do work previously done in-house
items.example: Outsourcing cleaning cut costs and loyalty in one stroke.

items.definitionEn: moving work to another country, usually to reduce costs
items.example: Offshoring the call centre sparked a local campaign.

items.definitionEn: the lowest hourly pay the law allows for most workers
items.example: The minimum wage rise still left rent out of reach in the city.

items.definitionEn: an hourly rate set higher than the legal minimum, meant to cover basic costs
items.example: The café pays the living wage and still cannot fill weekend shifts.

items.definitionEn: an invisible barrier that stops certain groups reaching top posts
items.example: The glass ceiling is still visible in the partnership figures.

items.definitionEn: the pattern of appointing women to leadership only when an organisation is already in crisis
items.example: She recognised a glass cliff when they offered her the failing unit.

items.definitionEn: exhaustion and loss of motivation after prolonged workplace stress
items.example: Burnout pushed him to a four-day week.

items.definitionPl: równowaga między pracą a życiem prywatnym
items.definitionEn: a sustainable division of time and energy between job and private life
items.example: A sixty-hour week destroyed her work-life balance.

items.definitionEn: a risk that comes with a particular job
items.example: Hearing loss is an occupational hazard in some workshops.

items.definitionEn: money paid to an employee when a job ends, especially in redundancy
items.example: Severance pay covered three months while she retrained.

items.definitionEn: the legal minimum an employer must pay when you are off work because of illness
items.example: Statutory sick pay is far below her usual monthly income.

items.definitionEn: time off work around the birth of a child for the mother
items.example: Maternity leave can be shared in part with the other parent.

items.definitionEn: time off work for a father or partner around a child's birth
items.example: Two weeks of paternity leave is still the legal minimum.

items.definitionEn: unpaid or paid time off to care for a child, available to eligible parents
items.example: Parental leave must be requested well before the intended dates.

items.definitionEn: time away from work that is agreed but not paid
items.example: She took unpaid leave to finish the language course.

items.definitionEn: paid holiday entitlement for a year of work
items.example: Book annual leave before the school holidays fill up.

items.definitionEn: a retirement savings scheme arranged through the employer
items.example: Enrolment in the workplace pension is automatic unless you opt out.

items.definitionEn: extras besides wages, such as meals, insurance or a travel card
items.example: Fringe benefits made up for a modest basic salary.

items.definitionEn: informal extras that come with a particular role
items.example: Free rail travel is one of the perks of the job.

items.definitionEn: pay that rises or falls with measured results
items.example: Performance-related pay can pit colleagues against one another.

items.definitionEn: pay calculated as a percentage of sales or deals
items.example: Half her income is sales commission, so a quiet month hurts.

items.definitionEn: what you actually receive after tax and other deductions
items.example: Take-home pay barely covers the commute and lunch.

items.definitionEn: an increase in wages or salary
items.example: The union asked for a pay rise matching inflation.

items.definitionEn: a period when wages are not increased
items.example: A two-year pay freeze felt like a cut in real terms.

items.definitionPl: luka płacowa ze względu na płeć
items.definitionEn: the difference between average pay of men and women in an organisation or economy
items.example: The gender pay gap widened among part-time staff.

items.definitionPl: równa płaca za tę samą pracę
items.definitionEn: the principle that people doing the same work should receive the same pay
items.example: Equal pay claims forced the council to review job grades.

items.definitionEn: free time given instead of extra pay for additional hours worked
items.example: Weekend duty is compensated with time off in lieu, not cash.

items.definitionEn: the amount of work a person or team is expected to complete
items.example: An impossible workload is a health-and-safety issue, not a badge of honour.

items.definitionPl: godziny pracy kolidujące z życiem społecznym
items.definitionEn: working times that clash with evenings, nights or weekends
items.example: Anti-social hours in hospitals are paid at a higher rate.

items.definitionEn: available to work if needed, often outside normal hours
items.example: Doctors who are on call may still be woken twice a night.

items.definitionEn: harmful pressure caused by the demands of a job
items.example: Occupational stress is a recognised cause of long-term sick leave.

items.definitionEn: pain or damage from repeating the same movement at work
items.example: Repetitive strain injury from typing forced her to change role.

items.definitionEn: rules and practices that protect people from harm at work
items.example: Health and safety training is compulsory before you enter the warehouse.

items.definitionEn: clothing or gear worn to reduce workplace injury, such as helmets or goggles
items.example: Protective equipment is useless if staff are not trained to use it.

items.definitionEn: repeated hostile behaviour towards someone at work
items.example: Workplace bullying thrives where managers look away.

items.definitionEn: resigning because the employer has made staying intolerable, treated in law as a dismissal
items.example: A sudden pay cut can amount to constructive dismissal.

items.definitionEn: being sacked without a fair reason or a fair procedure
items.example: Unfair dismissal claims go to an employment tribunal.

items.definitionEn: the official steps for raising a complaint at work
items.example: Use the grievance procedure in writing and keep copies.

items.definitionEn: the official steps an employer follows when alleging misconduct
items.example: The disciplinary procedure allows a colleague to accompany you.

items.definitionEn: a person who reports serious wrongdoing in an organisation
items.example: The whistleblower was later protected by statute.

items.definitionEn: unwanted conduct that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment
items.example: Harassment includes comments as well as physical behaviour.

items.definitionEn: unfair treatment because of a protected characteristic such as age or disability
items.example: Discrimination at work can be subtle in promotion decisions.

items.definitionEn: fair treatment in hiring, pay and advancement regardless of personal characteristics
items.example: Workplace equality training is mandatory for anyone on a panel.

items.definitionEn: practical changes an employer must consider so a disabled person can work
items.example: Reasonable adjustments included a quieter desk and flexible start times.

items.definitionEn: to leave a job by your own decision
items.example: She will resign once the project is handed over.

items.definitionEn: to end someone's job because the role is no longer needed
items.example: The plant will make redundant eighty night-shift staff.

items.definitionEn: to stop working, usually because of age or a pension
items.example: He plans to retire at sixty-five and tutor part-time.

items.definitionEn: the pay and support offered when posts are abolished
items.example: The redundancy package included retraining and outplacement.

items.definitionEn: choosing to leave in a round of job cuts, usually with extra pay
items.example: Older staff took voluntary redundancy rather than relocate.

items.definitionEn: leaving work before the usual pension age, sometimes with a reduced pension
items.example: Early retirement was offered to anyone over fifty-eight.

items.definitionEn: an agreed period away from paid work, often to care for family or retrain
items.example: A career break to raise children need not end a profession.

items.definitionEn: an extended period of leave, often unpaid, for study or rest, then a return to the same employer
items.example: A six-month sabbatical let her finish the language diploma.

items.definitionEn: to formally tell your employer you are leaving
items.example: Hand in your notice only after the new contract is signed.

items.definitionEn: a meeting when you leave, used to hear why you are going
items.example: In the exit interview she named the impossible targets.

items.definitionEn: a large payment to someone leaving a senior post
items.example: The golden handshake caused anger while junior staff faced cuts.

items.definitionPl: outplacement, pomoc w znalezieniu nowej pracy
items.definitionEn: support from the old employer to help redundant staff find new work
items.example: Outplacement included CV workshops and interview practice.

items.definitionEn: moving staff to another job in the same organisation instead of dismissing them
items.example: Redeployment saved some warehouse roles after automation.

items.definitionEn: reducing the number of staff to cut costs
items.example: Downsizing was announced as a 'restructuring' in the same email.

items.definitionEn: to end someone's employment, typically for conduct or capability
items.example: The firm may dismiss an employee only after a fair hearing.

items.definitionEn: an organisation of workers that bargains over pay and conditions
items.example: Join a trade union before you need it, not after a dispute starts.

items.definitionEn: to stop work collectively as a protest over pay or conditions
items.example: Nurses voted to go on strike after talks collapsed.

items.definitionEn: a line of striking workers outside a workplace, asking others not to enter
items.example: Deliveries turned away at the picket line.

items.definitionEn: collective measures by workers, including strikes and work-to-rule
items.example: Industrial action delayed trains for a fortnight.

items.definitionEn: negotiations between unions and employers over pay and conditions for a group
items.example: Collective bargaining set the pay scale for the whole plant.

items.definitionPl: mąż zaufania, przedstawiciel związku w zakładzie
items.definitionEn: a union representative elected by workers in a particular workplace
items.example: The shop steward sat in on the disciplinary meeting.

items.definitionEn: when an employer stops workers from entering until a dispute is settled
items.example: The lockout lasted ten days before talks resumed.

items.definitionEn: a binding decision on a dispute by an independent third party
items.example: Both sides agreed to arbitration rather than another strike.

items.definitionEn: doing only what the contract strictly requires, as a form of protest
items.example: A work-to-rule slowed the airport to a crawl.

items.definitionEn: a union instruction not to work extra hours as a form of protest
items.example: The overtime ban left shelves empty by Sunday.

items.definitionEn: a serious disagreement between workers and employers over work
items.example: The labour dispute began with unpaid weekend shifts.

items.definitionEn: a person chosen to speak for union members in talks with management
items.example: Ask a union representative to read the new contract.

items.definitionEn: a vote among members on whether to take strike action
items.example: The strike ballot passed the legal turnout threshold.

items.definitionEn: the activity of starting and running businesses, taking on financial risk
items.example: The school now teaches entrepreneurship alongside accountancy.

items.definitionEn: a newly founded company, often in technology, still finding its market
items.example: The start-up ran out of cash before the product launched.

items.definitionEn: a person who sets up a business and takes on its risks
items.example: The entrepreneur sold the firm after five years.

items.definitionEn: a written outline of how a venture will work, cost and earn money
items.example: The bank refused a loan without a business plan.

items.definitionEn: investment in young companies in return for a share of ownership
items.example: Venture capital came with a seat on the board.

items.definitionEn: the first money used to start a company, often from founders or angels
items.example: Seed funding paid for the prototype and six months' rent.

items.definitionEn: a person who runs a business as an individual, fully liable for debts
items.example: As a sole trader she pays tax on profits, not through PAYE.

items.definitionEn: a firm whose owners' liability is limited to what they invested
items.example: They formed a limited company before taking on staff.

items.definitionEn: a business owned by two or more people who share profits and liability
items.example: The partnership broke up when one partner emigrated.

items.definitionEn: running outlets under another company's brand, following its rules, in return for fees
items.example: Franchising is expensive to buy into and tightly controlled.

items.definitionEn: to earn more money than you spend in a period
items.example: The shop did not turn a profit until the second summer.

items.definitionEn: to make neither a loss nor a profit
items.example: The café should break even within eighteen months.

items.definitionEn: the movement of money in and out of a business
items.example: Poor cash flow, not a lack of orders, sank the workshop.

items.definitionEn: regular costs of running a business, such as rent and utilities
items.example: High overheads in the old town killed the bookshop.

items.definitionEn: a small, specialised group of customers
items.example: They survived by serving a niche market of vintage-camera buyers.

items.definitionEn: gathering information about customers and competitors before you sell
items.example: Market research showed the app had no paying audience.

items.definitionEn: a feature that lets a business outperform rivals in a market
items.example: Same-day repairs became their competitive advantage.

items.definitionEn: a short persuasive talk aimed at winning a customer or investor
items.example: The sales pitch lasted three minutes and no longer.

items.definitionEn: to grow a business in size while keeping the model working
items.example: They could not scale up without a second warehouse.

items.definitionEn: to start the legal process of being declared unable to pay your debts
items.example: If the loan is refused they will file for bankruptcy by winter.

items.definitionEn: the state of being unable to pay debts as they fall due
items.example: Insolvency advisers were called in before Christmas.

items.definitionEn: anyone with an interest in an organisation, including staff, customers and neighbours
items.example: Residents are a stakeholder in the factory's night-shift plans.

items.definitionEn: a person or body that owns shares in a company
items.example: Each shareholder received a letter about the dividend.

items.definitionEn: the profit from money put into a venture, relative to what was spent
items.example: The return on investment was lower than a savings account.

items.definitionEn: paid work done besides a main job
items.example: Her side hustle in evening tutoring paid the energy bills.

items.definitionEn: earning a living from several part-time roles or clients at once
items.example: A portfolio career mixed teaching, translating and examining.

items.definitionEn: a shared office rented by freelancers and small firms
items.example: The coworking space was cheaper than a private office.

items.definitionEn: a system in which staff start and finish at different times to spread demand
items.example: Staggered hours eased crowding on the morning trains.

items.definitionEn: being out of work and looking for a job for a year or more
items.example: Long-term unemployment is hardest on people over fifty.

items.definitionEn: a person who is looking for paid work
items.example: Each jobseeker must show evidence of applications.

items.definitionEn: having a job that uses too few hours or too little of your skill
items.example: Underemployment among graduates is as painful as open unemployment.

items.definitionEn: how safe your post is from sudden loss
items.example: Job security vanished when the plant went onto rolling contracts.

items.definitionEn: insecure employment with unstable hours, pay or rights
items.example: Precarious work has spread from hospitality into teaching.

items.definitionEn: the sequence of more senior posts in a field
items.example: The career ladder in nursing is clearer than in publishing.

items.definitionEn: a post with no real chance of progress or skill growth
items.example: He left a dead-end job to train as an electrician.

items.definitionEn: to record the time you finish work, often on a machine
items.example: Staff must not clock off until the handover is complete.

items.definitionEn: the part of the day when flexitime staff must be at work
items.example: Core hours are ten until three in this office.

items.definitionEn: a specialist court that hears disputes about work rights
items.example: She took the case to an employment tribunal and won compensation.

items.definitionEn: training existing staff in additional skills for current or future tasks
items.example: Upskilling the warehouse team reduced the need for agency staff.

items.definitionEn: training people for a different kind of work after their old role disappears
items.example: Reskilling coal workers for renewable energy is slow and expensive.

items.definitionEn: learning a role by doing it under supervision, rather than in a classroom
items.example: On-the-job training covered the till on the first morning.
